description: Planning a deck and a fence for the same Middle Tennessee yard? Line up the stairs with the gate, pair the wood and stain, and check the rules first.

sections.heading: Planning a deck and a fence for the same yard
paragraphs: If you want both, plan them together, even if one gets built months after the other. The deck stairs decide where people step into the yard, and that path usually ends at a gate. A fence line drawn on its own can put the gate far from where the stairs come down. Sketch both on one drawing of the lot so the gate sits on the path you will actually walk.

In many yards it makes sense to build the deck first. Deck lumber and the equipment for digging footings have to reach the backyard, and on most lots they come through a side yard. Once a fence closes that side, everything has to fit through a gate. If the fence has to come first, say because a dog needs a yard now, plan a gate wide enough for materials to pass. A drive gate can do that job, and later it lets a mower or a trailer through.

sections.heading: Choosing materials and heights that work together
paragraphs: The deck and the fence do not need to be the same material, but they should look like they were chosen together. Cedar and pressure treated pine weather differently, so a bare cedar fence beside a bare pine deck usually will not match in color. Using the same stain on both helps, though the two woods take stain a little differently, so test it on a scrap of each first. Composite deck boards come in set colors and generally are not stained. With composite, pick a fence stain close to the deck color instead of chasing an exact match.

A raised deck changes what a fence can hide. Standing on the deck, you are above the yard, and a privacy fence of the usual height may not block your view into the yard next door. When privacy up on the deck matters, a screen along one side of the deck often does more than a taller fence. Many cities and HOAs cap fence height anyway, and the limits vary by address. Read more about [raised decks on sloped lots](/decks/) and [choosing a privacy fence style](/fences/).

sections.heading: What to gather before you ask for an estimate
paragraphs: Photos taken after a hard rain are worth having. They show where water sits, which matters for deck footings and for the bottom of a fence. Find your survey or plat too. It shows where the lot lines run and whether an easement crosses the yard, and you may have gotten a copy with the closing papers when you bought the house. The guide on [fences and property lines](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) explains why the lines come first.

In an HOA, pull the covenants and the architectural guidelines before anything is drawn, and find out how the committee wants requests sent in. Knowing the limits on fence height and stain color early keeps the plan from being drawn twice. It also helps to note anything buried that the 811 utility locators usually do not mark, since they mark lines that member utilities own and not private ones like sprinkler lines or septic lines. For the submission itself, see the [HOA approval guide](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/).

faqs.q: Do you build both decks and fences?
faqs.a: Yes, we build both, and one request covers them. In the estimate form at the bottom of this page, choose Deck and fence as the project type, then use the notes box to describe each part. Planning them in one conversation makes it easier to line up the deck stairs with a gate and to pick finishes that suit each other.

We work across Middle Tennessee. The cities we serve are listed on our [service areas page](/service-areas/), and each one has its own page about the ground and local rules there. If your town is not on that list, the ZIP code field in the estimate form is how we confirm whether your address is in our area.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a deck or a fence?
faqs.a: Decks need one more often than fences do. A deck attached to the house or built well off the ground typically needs a permit and inspections. Fence rules vary more from town to town, and some places do not require a fence permit at all. HOA approval is a separate step from any permit. Confirm the rules for your address with the city or county codes office, and see our [deck permit guide](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) for how the process usually works.

faqs.q: How do I get an estimate?
faqs.a: Start with the form at the bottom of this page. Pick the kind of project and add your ZIP code so we can confirm your address is in our area. Use the notes box for anything else we should know, like an old fence or deck that has to come out first. Once you send it, we get back to you to talk the project through.
